LanceDB Raises $57.5M Series B to Expand Its Multimodal AI Lakehouse
Published

By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent

Key Points LanceDB raised $57.5 million to expand a lakehouse that curates and serves AI training…

LanceDB raised $57.5 million to expand a lakehouse that curates and serves AI training data.
The company reports more than tenfold year-over-year revenue growth since its Series A in June 2025.
LanceDB aims to unify training data, experiments and rollouts so teams stop hand-managing pipelines.
LanceDB announced on November 17, 2026 that it raised $57.5 million in Series B funding to expand its multimodal lakehouse, a platform for organizing and delivering AI training data. The round brings the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.
Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the round, with participation from Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator. LanceDB plans to put the capital toward a broader role across model development, including training-data management, feature engineering, experiment execution and data loading.
Adoption and Technical Scale
LanceDB says researchers can lose weeks or months obtaining and curating training data even though frontier AI advances are measured in days and weeks. Its multimodal lakehouse is intended to close that gap by combining curation, search and retrieval, feature engineering and training for work on frontier models, world models, physical AI and enterprise applications.
The company reports more than tenfold year-over-year revenue growth since its Series A in June 2025. Its open-source library has been downloaded more than 120 million times, representing sixfold growth in total downloads from the same point a year earlier. Customers include Netflix, Microsoft AI, Runway , Luma AI and Midjourney.
The platform is designed to hold multimodal data such as videos, images and sensor data while supporting large-scale retrieval and training. LanceDB says the platform supports more than 130,000 requests per second with latency below 210 milliseconds for 95% of requests, individual tables containing hundreds of petabytes of data or more than 40 billion vectors, and training across 8,000 GPUs in parallel.
Enterprise additions address updates to those tables while they are in use. A durable, memory-accelerated write path handles real-time ingest, distributed indexing scales across large datasets, and managed compaction continuously optimizes tables in the background. LanceDB says managed compaction supports up to 100 billion multimodal rows while multiple researchers concurrently read, write and query the same table.
Customers Describe Changing Training Datasets
Runway CTO Kamil Sindi described how one training example evolves: “A training example at Runway doesn’t stay still. It starts as a video and a prompt, then we add embeddings, resolution and duration metadata, whatever the next experiment needs.” Runway began using the Lance data format in 2024 and later became a LanceDB Enterprise customer. The company now uses Lance and LanceDB Enterprise together so researchers can work through large, changing datasets more quickly.

The post Systems Planning And Analysis Receives Up To $55.7 Million Navy Trident II Support Order appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
articles.text:
Systems Planning And Analysis Receives Up To $55.7 Million Navy Trident II Support Order
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 10:45 AM
Systems Planning And Analysis Receives Up To $55.7 Million Navy Trident II Support Order
Systems Planning and Analysis has received a Navy task order valued at up to approximately $55.7 million to support the Trident II Strategic Weapons System.
The Alexandria, Virginia-based company will perform technical assessments and studies, systems engineering and analysis, program integration, and schedule support.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee term task order is identified as N0003027F3024. Its $55.7 million stated value includes optional line items, meaning the full amount depends on whether the Navy exercises those options.
Work is expected to continue through September 30, 2031. Washington, D.C., will account for 60% of performance, while Alexandria will account for 32%.
The remaining work will be distributed among Bangor, Washington; Denver, Colorado; Titusville, Florida; Kings Bay, Georgia; Pittsfield, Massachusetts; Valley Forge, Pennsylvania; Magna, Utah; and Sunnyvale, California. Each location represents 1% of performance.
Initial obligations total approximately $1.7 million. This includes $200,981 in fiscal 2026 research, development, test, and evaluation funding; $150,000 in fiscal 2027 RDT&E funding; and approximately $1.3 million in fiscal 2027 Navy operation and maintenance funding.
The $200,981 fiscal 2026 RDT&E allocation will expire at the end of fiscal 2027. The source announcement does not state that the remaining potential task-order value has been obligated.
The effort also benefits a foreign military sale to the United Kingdom, reflecting the U.K.’s role in the Trident strategic weapons enterprise.
The task order will be issued as a sole-source acquisition under an authority associated with federal small-business research and development programs.
Portfolio Acquisition Executive, Strategic Systems Programs in Washington, D.C., is the contracting activity. Strategic Systems Programs manages the Navy’s sea-based strategic deterrence systems.

articles.title: AI-Native CRM Dreamteam Raises $53 Million in Seed and Series A Funding
articles.snippet: AI-Native CRM Dreamteam Raises $53 Million in Seed and Series A Funding Wowtale
articles.text:
For more than two decades, CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot have depended on salespeople remembering to type in what happened on a call. When they forget, customer context disappears and the pipeline fills with stale data. Dreamteam , an AI-native CRM built on the opposite premise, said it raised $53 million from Accel, Together Fund and Premji Invest. The company described the amount as seed and Series A funding combined and did not disclose a valuation.
A CRM that fills itself from conversations
At the center of Dreamteam is what it calls the Company Brain, a running memory built from customer conversations, emails, meetings and workflows. It pulls out buyer intent, objections, competitor mentions and stakeholder dynamics. The company argues that legacy CRMs, built around structured fields and hand-coded workflows, cannot hold signals like a prospect hesitating on price or a board suddenly scrutinizing costs. It says an account that changes hands carries over the customer’s goals, objections and open commitments.
Four AI teammates work on top of that memory. Rachel is a research assistant that enriches accounts and contacts. Sally, the sales assistant, preps meetings, drafts follow-up emails and manages tasks. Raj is a RevOps partner that monitors the pipeline, flags at-risk deals and improves forecasts. Alex is a CRM administrator that configures the system from plain-language requests. The company says customers do not have to build or train their own agents.
Humans keep control. A person has to approve any outgoing email, teams set pricing rules and approval limits, and users can see where a recommendation came from and correct what the system remembers. Alongside the human interface, Dreamteam offers an API and a Model Context Protocol server so AI agents such as Claude or ChatGPT can reach the CRM. A feature called Magic Apps lets business users build apps and dashboards in natural language.
The company says more than 100 companies in 13 countries use it, and its press release puts the figure at hundreds across AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting. Named customers include invideo, Plex and DMS Health. invideo started with a small pilot and expanded to its whole sales team, and Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer called its compatibility with existing AI tools like Claude “a game changer.” Revenue and pricing were not disclosed.
Three former Freshworks executives
The co-founders are former senior executives at Freshworks. CEO Anand Venkatraman leads sales and go-to-market, Ramesh Parthasarathy leads engineering and Senthil Kanthaswamy leads product. The company says they helped scale Freshworks from its early startup days through its IPO and have built AI applications since the GPT-2 era, scaling them to tens of thousands of businesses. When AI reasoning made it possible for software to understand context and carry out work, they decided to rebuild CRM from scratch rather than layer AI onto existing systems. Dreamteam was founded in 2025 and says it is headquartered in Sacramento, California.
Its blog post names Together Fund and Accel as leads, with Premji Invest participating. Together Fund, founded by Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham, is Dreamteam’s first institutional investor. Mathrubootham said the cloud wave created a generation of enterprise software leaders 25 years ago and that AI demands software rebuilt from the ground up, with CRM among the largest categories ripe for disruption

articles.title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
articles.snippet: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM TechCrunch
articles.text:
Dreamteam , a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.
Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.
Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.
That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.
At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.
Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.
The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”
Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

articles.title: Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
articles.snippet:
Arcturus Therapeutics has expanded its collaboration with Meiji Seika Pharma through a $50 million equity investment, an additional technology license and a proposed pandemic preparedness partnership in Japan.
The post Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
articles.text:
Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 4:20 PM
Arcturus Therapeutics Secures $50 Million Meiji Investment At 80% Premium
Arcturus Therapeutics has expanded its collaboration with Meiji Seika Pharma through a $50 million equity investment, an additional technology license and a proposed pandemic preparedness partnership in Japan.
Meiji will purchase unregistered Arcturus securities at $20.27 per share, an 80% premium under the announced transaction terms. Its investment will represent approximately 7.9% of outstanding shares following the transaction.
The companies also signed an exclusive license covering the application of Arcturus’s ARCT-154 technology in an undisclosed therapeutic area.
Separately, a memorandum of understanding establishes principal terms for a potential collaboration and license agreement involving pandemic preparedness and response in Japan. That arrangement remains subject to a definitive agreement.
Arcturus intends to use the investment to support its cystic fibrosis program and accelerate ARCT-2601, an investigational treatment for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.
ARCT-2601 is the first mRNA therapeutic intended to use the company’s LUNAR 2.0 delivery platform. Its development is expected to contribute to clinical evaluation of that next-generation technology.
President and CEO Joseph Payne said the expanded relationship reflects Meiji’s confidence in the company’s capabilities and platform.
Founded in 2013 and based in San Diego, Arcturus develops mRNA medicines focused on liver and respiratory diseases.
Its technologies include lipid-mediated delivery and self-amplifying RNA. The company also developed KOSTAIVE, a self-amplifying mRNA COVID vaccine.
Other collaborations include work with Thermo Fisher Scientific, BARDA and Japanese manufacturing joint venture ARCALIS.
Meiji’s investment adds capital while extending an existing strategic relationship across development, licensing and potential public-health applications.
The company’s pipeline programs remain subject to clinical development, regulatory review and other requirements before potential commercialization.
KEY QUOTES
“We are pleased to expand our relationship with Meiji as we advance innovative mRNA medicines and seek to deliver value to patients. The investment, together with the license agreement and the pandemic preparedness MOU, reflects Meiji’s confidence in our development capabilities and the potential of our technology platform. Alongside our CF program, these proceeds will be used to accelerate development of ARCT-2601 for OTC deficiency, the first mRNA therapeutic to utilize our LUNAR 2.0 delivery platform.”
Joseph Payne, President And CEO Of Arcturus Therapeutics

Led by Blue Cloud Ventures, the round brings total funding to $96 million, with more than 1,500 dealerships across the U.S. and Canada already running on Numa's AI Operating System
SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Numa , the AI Operating System for dealerships, today announced a $45 million Series C led by Blue Cloud Ventures, with participation from Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures and Tokio Marine Future Fund. The round brings Numa's total funding to $96 million. It caps a year in which Numa tripled in size, tripled its annual recurring revenue and became the AI system GM, FordDirect, BMW and Stellantis each put in front of their dealerships.
Numa has already won the hardest part of the dealership: the customer conversation. The system has handled more than 1 billion calls, texts and chats and booked more than 4 million appointments. Dealerships that run on Numa stay and grow with it. Net revenue retention has risen over the past year, and more dealerships are moving to longer agreements.
For decades, dealership software was built one task at a time. Each system kept its own record of what happened, and none of them acted on what the customer just said. The first wave of AI did not change that. It answered faster, then handed the work back to people to chase by hand.
Numa does not hand the work back. It knows not just who the customer is but what they need, and it acts on it: booking the visit, finding the right car, routing the call or flagging the customer about to leave.
"In two years, every general manager will have an AI COO," said Tasso Roumeliotis, founder and CEO of Numa. "At more than 1,500 dealerships, they already do, and it is Numa. It knows every conversation in the store, sees what needs attention and runs the work that follows. That is not another dashboard or another point tool. It is an operating system. The DMS was built to record the dealership. It was never built to run it. Numa was, and this round puts more engineers to accelerate it."
"What is unique about Numa is that the company understands the DNA and culture of a dealership and seamlessly AI-enables the workflow while empowering all constituents including the dealerships customers", added Mir Arif, Managing Partner of Blue Cloud Ventures. "Numa is not prescriptive but rather deeply understands the objectives of the BDC representative, the salesperson, the service technician, the parts specialist and the sales manager and significantly enhances their productivity."
"As an insurer, we view dealerships as a critical part of the ecosystem that supports customers throughout their vehicle ownership journey," said Mitsutoshi Shizuru, Managing Executive Officer of Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance Co., Ltd, "Numa is using AI to make this important customer touchpoint faster, more efficient, and more seamless. We believe Numa's technology has the potential to revolutionize the relationship between dealerships and their customers and help shape the next generation of mobility customer experiences in the U.S. and beyond."

Mount Thor, a start-up specialising in Apple-based computing infrastructure, has raised US$45 million through two funding rounds as it looks to expand its data centre services for artificial intelligence (AI) agents.
The company operates racks of Apple computers that provide remote access to macOS environments for businesses, developers and AI research teams. Its approach addresses the growing need for computing infrastructure that can run tasks that depend on Apple’s operating system and applications.
As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks through computer interfaces, access to traditional cloud infrastructure may not always be sufficient. Some applications and workflows require macOS-specific features, creating demand for dedicated Mac environments that can be accessed remotely.
Mount Thor aims to meet this demand by providing businesses with managed access to Mac hardware without requiring them to purchase, maintain and operate large fleets of Apple computers themselves. The funding will support the company’s infrastructure expansion, recruitment and research into running AI models on Apple silicon.
Mount Thor targets the growing demand for Mac-based AI infrastructure
AI agents are increasingly being developed to interact with computers like human users. Rather than simply responding to written instructions, these systems can navigate software, manage files, operate applications and complete tasks through graphical interfaces.
Some agents are designed to work independently for extended periods, while others respond to requests as they arrive. These capabilities create new infrastructure requirements, particularly when agents need access to desktop environments to perform their assigned work.
However, conventional cloud computing systems do not always provide the software compatibility these operations require. Applications designed specifically for macOS, along with features available through Apple’s ecosystem, can make Mac hardware necessary for certain development and deployment tasks.
Mount Thor provides remotely accessible Mac systems that let organisations create and run these environments without managing the physical equipment. The service targets research laboratories, software developers, and companies building AI-powered platforms.
Research teams could use the infrastructure to create different computing environments to evaluate AI models. This is especially relevant for systems trained to understand and control software through visual interfaces, where testing requires access to real desktop environments.
Businesses developing autonomous agent platforms could also use Mount Thor’s machines to provide individual macOS workspaces. These environments could remain active for weeks, allowing agents to keep working on tasks without a human physically operating a computer.
